Increased risk of bradycardia and sedation. Manufacturers of clonidine often contraindicate concomitant methylphenidate in their summaries of product characteristics. This is based on a few reported suspected deaths from the mid-1990s. The causal relationship must be regarded as very uncertain, and clonidine alone is also known to cause cardiac arrhythmias. Subsequently, there have been no further reports despite continued use of the combination. It has therefore been argued that the evidence as a whole must be regarded as inconclusive regarding a possible serious interaction risk. In addition, there are study data showing that combining methylphenidate and clonidine may have beneficial effects that are not achieved with either agent alone, without an increased risk of serious adverse effects.

In some settings, the bleeding risk has been shown to increase (for example in the RE-LY study, where the bleeding risk with dabigatran doubled when low-dose acetylsalicylic acid or other antiplatelet agents were given concomitantly). Studies with direct factor Xa inhibitors such as rivaroxaban have also shown that combination with low-dose acetylsalicylic acid increases the bleeding risk. As a general precaution, it is reasonable to avoid high-dose acetylsalicylic acid altogether, since good alternatives exist.

One of the mechanisms of action of tramadol is to stimulate the serotonin system, and possibly also activity in the pain-inhibiting serotonergic pathways in the CNS. This effect may be blocked by 5-HT3 antagonists. The increased dose of tramadol that must be given to compensate for this will lead to an increased tendency to nausea and a reduced effect of the 5-HT3 antagonist.
